title: A Heap Is a Shape and an Order, Not a Sorted Tree
quickIdea: A binary heap is two requirements at once: a complete binary tree, with every level full except possibly the last and the last filled from the left, and a parent-child order, with every parent at least (max-heap) or at most (min-heap) each of its children. Either requirement alone is not a heap.
remember: Shape: all levels are full except possibly the last, and the last level is filled from the left with no gap. That is why a heap is never a chain, and why its height is only floor(log2 n).
Order: in a max-heap every parent is at least its two children; in a min-heap at most. Only parent-child pairs are constrained, so siblings and the two subtrees are unordered among themselves.
The order is non-strict, so equal keys are allowed: a parent holding 5 above a child holding 5 satisfies a max-heap.
The two requirements are independent. A complete tree with unsorted keys breaks the order; a chain whose every parent beats its children breaks the shape.

The root holds the maximum of all keys (max-heap) or the minimum (min-heap), so find-max or find-min is O(1). Nothing else about the arrangement is promised: a heap is neither sorted nor a search tree.
Testing an array costs one comparison per edge: check A[i] against A[2i] and A[2i+1] for every i, which is n-1 comparisons in O(n).

example.work: Read the array as a complete tree with 1-based indices, so node i has children 2i and 2i+1. First array: 23 beats 17 and 14; 17 beats 7 and 13; 14 beats 10 and 1; 7 beats 5 and 6; 13 beats 12. Every edge holds, so it is a max-heap. Second array: node 3 holds 10 and its child at index 6 holds 14, so the edge (3,6) runs upward and the order fails.
example.answer: The first is a max-heap. The second is not: the violation is the edge between index 3 (10) and index 6 (14).

gateAngle: GATE CSE 2023 Q.2 and GATE CSE 2009 Q.59 are the same question in different clothes: four arrays, one of which is a heap. Test each array against A[2i] and A[2i+1], stop at the first violation, and the option that survives every edge is the answer. The shape never needs drawing, because level order already fixes it.

variations.label: VERIFIED PYQ
variations.question: GATE CSE 2023 Q.2. Which one of the following sequences, when stored in an array at locations A[1] to A[10], forms a max-heap? (1) 23,17,10,6,13,14,1,5,7,12 (2) 23,17,14,7,13,10,1,5,6,12 (3) 23,17,14,6,13,10,1,5,7,15 (4) 23,14,17,1,10,13,16,12,7,5
variations.why: Option 1 fails at the edge (3,6): 10 is the parent of 14. Option 3 fails at (4,9): 6 is the parent of 15. Option 4 fails at (4,8): 1 is the parent of 12. Option 2 satisfies every edge: 23 over 17 and 14, 17 over 7 and 13, 14 over 10 and 1, 7 over 5 and 6, 13 over 12.

variations.label: CONCEPTUAL PRACTICE QUESTION
variations.question: Is [50,30,40,10,20,35,25] a max-heap? What changes if the 30 is replaced by 55?
variations.answer: It is a max-heap. With 55 at index 2 it is not, because 55 sits above 50.
variations.why: Edges of the first array: 50 over 30 and 40, 30 over 10 and 20, 40 over 35 and 25, all satisfied. Replacing 30 by 55 breaks the single edge (1,2), since the parent 50 is then smaller than its child. One edge is enough to decide, which is why these questions are answered in seconds.

trap.what: Reading a heap as if it were a search tree or a sorted array.
trap.why: The heap order constrains parent-child pairs only, so an inorder walk of a heap is not sorted and a search for an arbitrary key has no single branch to follow. Any reasoning that assumes the left subtree holds smaller keys is wrong here.
trap.counterexample: [7,4,6,1,3,2,5] is a valid max-heap, yet its inorder traversal is 1,4,3,7,2,6,5, which is not sorted; the left subtree of the root contains 4 and 3, both larger than the 2 sitting in the right subtree. So a heap is not a binary search tree, whatever the picture suggests.

check.question: Is [5,5,4,3,2,4,1] a max-heap?
check.explanation: Edges: 5 over 5 and 4; 5 over 3 and 2; 4 over 4 and 1. Every parent is at least each child, and equal keys are allowed because the order is non-strict. A common reflex is to reject the array because of the repeated 5 or the repeated 4; duplicates never violate a heap.
